platforms.title: 3 Signs That Separate Costochondritis From Angina
platforms.meta_description: Sharp chest pain and jumping straight to worrying about your heart? How cardiologists describe costochondritis versus angina, and when to call emergency care.
platforms.body_html:
Sharp chest pain and jumping straight to worrying it's your heart? Cardiologists explain that costochondritis and angina come from completely different places in the chest and behave differently. This article is general information, not a self-diagnosis tool — new or severe chest pain always deserves a proper medical evaluation.

Why the same general area produces such different pain

Costochondritis is inflammation of the cartilage connecting the ribs to the breastbone. The pain is usually sharply localized to one spot, and pressing on that exact spot or twisting the torso often reproduces it. It commonly follows intense exercise, repetitive movement, or a recent cold or viral infection.

Angina comes from an entirely different mechanism. It's marked by reduced blood flow to the heart muscle, producing a pressure-like, squeezing tightness in the center of the chest. Pressing on the chest doesn't reproduce it the same way, and the pain often spreads to the left arm, jaw, or back.

How to tell them apart, and what to check

First, whether shortness of breath, cold sweats, or nausea come along with it. Cardiologists point to these as classic companions of angina. Costochondritis almost never brings any of them along.

Second, whether it worsens with exertion, like climbing stairs, and eases with rest. Angina is closely tied to physical activity level and often settles within a few minutes of resting. Costochondritis reacts to specific postures or pressing on the area, but has little to do with overall activity level.

What matters most is never simply waiting it out at home when the two are hard to tell apart. The two can feel similar on their own, and if it's a first-time chest pain or there are risk factors like high blood pressure, diabetes, or smoking, angina can't be ruled out just because it seems like costochondritis. If the pain lasts more than 15 minutes, comes with shortness of breath, cold sweats, or spreads to the arm or jaw, calling emergency services or getting to an emergency room right away is the safe move.

When the distinction feels unclear, it helps to describe the exact location, whether pressing reproduces it, how it relates to movement, and any symptoms that came along with it, exactly as they happened, to medical staff. But none of that information should be used to decide against seeking care.

Stacked risk factors matter too. Having several of them together — smoking, high cholesterol, a family history of heart disease, being over 45 as a man or over 55 as a woman — raises suspicion for angina even when the pain otherwise seems reproducible by pressing on the chest wall. None of these factors alone rules anything in or out, but together they shift how urgently the pain should be taken.

At the emergency room, doctors don't rely on the symptom description alone either. An ECG and a blood test that checks for troponin, a protein released when heart muscle is under strain, are the standard way to confirm or rule out a cardiac cause within a short window of time, which is exactly why getting there quickly matters more than trying to work it out at home first.

Does pressing on the spot reproduce the pain exactly, or does it come with shortness of breath or spread toward your arm?
